**Re-asked at 1.0.13 on 2026-08-31, and the shape is narrower than this row said.** A plugin here is a *directory holding a manifest* -- `plugins/<name>/plugin.json` is loaded and `inspect` names it. A bare `plugins/<name>.js` is **not**: the same run reported `Plugins (0)` with one present, which is what the first probe of the day used before the control caught it. A row that says a directory is read and does not say what shape is read there is one somebody can satisfy and get nothing.

**And the vendor's own installer writes somewhere else.** `grok plugin install <dir> --trust` creates `~/.grok/installed-plugins/<name>-<hash>/` and `~/.grok/installed-plugins/registry.json`, and creates no `plugins/` at all. That pair is a unit: the same manifest placed under `installed-plugins/` *without* the registry loads nothing, measured as the control. So `installed-plugins` is a person's installed plugins and their record of them -- product-owned, now in `never_touch` for the reason `auth.json` is: no live leak while it sits outside every owned namespace, and a safety list that depends on a namespace never widening is one waiting for a declaration change.

**A person's marketplace record lives inside this namespace, and a posture switch took it.** Measured 2026-08-31 with the released binary against a temporary home: `plugin marketplace add <path>` records the source in `config.toml` under `[[marketplace.sources]]`, and the pinned bytes also join `plugins` to `known_marketplaces.json` -- six occurrences, beside `extraKnownMarketplaces` and the `~/.claude` compatibility settings names. Planting that file and running `select nddev-builder` then `select minimal` removed it, because replacement empties a namespace whole.

It is in `never_touch` now, and `never_touch` was made to mean it: the list named three effects of ownership and stopped two -- a backup does not capture and an identity does not hash -- while deletion went straight through. `remove_keeping` spares exactly the named path and nothing beside it, which a control in the same test asserts. This namespace routes the plugin kind, so it cannot be dropped the way cursor's redundant parent was.

**And a larger one this only narrows.** `config.toml` is owned whole, and the product writes a person's marketplace sources into it, so a posture switch still replaces that file entire. Owning a settings file whole is the estate's model and this is its cost, named here rather than left to be discovered: it wants fragment ownership keyed by table, which is a protocol change and not a note.

surfaces.note:
The product's own reference lists `~/.grok/rules/` as *Always scanned; applies to all projects*. Owned from 2026-08-28, having been neither owned nor recorded -- so a backup captures it and a restore returns it.

**Routing no kind, and the reason is a rule this repository enforces.** `instruction` already routes to the owned `AGENTS.md`, and one kind routed by two surfaces makes a consumer's route ambiguous -- the surfaces guard refuses it by name, which is how this row was written the first time and corrected. Both surfaces are real: `AGENTS.md` is the single global instruction document, `rules/` a directory of always-scanned rule files. Which of the two an `instruction` component should reach is a question for the per-kind route the consumer is building; until that exists there is no way to say it, and guessing would put a component in one of two places that both look right. Exercised 2026-08-28 by running `grok inspect` against a temporary GROK_HOME holding a marker component here; the product reports it back by name.

**Written down 2026-08-30 rather than left implying it is coming, and the consumer's measurement makes the reason stronger than this row put it.** This said one kind on two surfaces leaves a compiler choosing with nothing telling it how. The consumer measured its own lookup: `rule_for(component_type, harness_id)` scans its rule table and returns the **first** match. So a second row for one kind is not ambiguous-and-unresolved -- it is *unreachable, silently*. Nothing would refuse it and nothing would say it was skipped.

The inverse already works and is in that table: claude's `plugin` and `skill` both project to `skills` -- two kinds sharing one path, two lookups, no collision. One kind on two paths is the direction the lookup cannot express.

**And this is not waiting on a release.** Per-surface selection is not on the consumer's roadmap, and if it arrives it changes the component model rather than the table: a component would have to name its surface, which is a passport field and an architecture decision. So there is no consumer version to re-ask this against. Re-ask when a passport carries a surface name; the consumer will say when one does.

declined.reason:
An administrator's **signed** policy, and this build owned it until 2026-08-28. Owning it deleted it.

**Measured on the shipped 0.0.11 binary**, against a target holding a managed grok home: `install baseline` removed `managed_config.toml` and `requirements.toml` and **kept** `managed_config.sig.json`, `managed_identity.sig.json` and `managed_config_cache.json`. That is exactly the state the product's own gate refuses -- `xai_grok_config::managed_cache` carries *"refusing session -- the signed is-managed claim requires an authentic policy sidecar and none is present"* and *"refusing session on tamper evidence"*.

The harm was the **split**: owning the policy and not its sidecars left a signature with nothing to verify. `grok setup` writes all of them, server-fetched and signature-checked -- its own `--json` help exists so the command "writes nothing to `~/.grok`".

**The previous reason for owning it was circular.** It read *"owned so a backup returns it byte-exact after an operation touches the home"* -- and the only reason an operation touched it was that it was owned. `restore` does bring it back, measured; the person's next `grok` run happens before that and is refused. Now in `never_touch`: not deleted, not captured into a slot, not hashed into an identity.

**And there is a system layer above this one, outside any target.** `/etc/grok/managed_config.toml` and `/etc/grok/requirements.toml` are path literals in the pinned binary. They get no row of their own because every recorded path here is relative to the target and those are relative to a root this provider never evaluates against -- the guard refused the row when it was tried, correctly. Recorded in this sentence instead, the same way antigravity's `~/.cache/ms-playwright-go` is.

**It bears on the `full-auto` posture.** That setup writes `[ui] permission_mode = always-approve`; the product's own documentation puts the system layer at the top of the chain -- *"requirements.toml / MDM (org-enforced; clamps every config layer below, including the overlay)"*. So on a managed machine the setup installs, verifies and restores cleanly and changes nothing, which is the same defect class as a correct key under a wrong name.

surfaces.note:
**Run, not read.** The pinned `grok-1.0.13-linux-x86_64` was fetched, its digest checked against the artifact table, and driven with `grok inspect` -- *Show the configuration Grok discovers for this directory*, which needs no credential. With a `SKILL.md` at `$HOME/.agents/skills/nddev-user-root-probe/` it reports:

```
  Skills (1)
  └ nddev-user-root-probe  user
```

-- discovered, and at the **user** tier, which is the half the embedded reference's tier table asserted and a run confirms.

**With a control.** A second skill at `$HOME/.agents-not-a-root/skills/` -- a sibling root no page names -- is absent: the count is 1, not 2. Without it, "the probe was found" could not be told from "the product scans `$HOME`".

The one root in this estate that belongs to a convention rather than to a product. `$HOME/.agents/skills` is a *sibling* of this product's configuration home, not a child, so nothing declared against this provider's own target can reach it -- that is what `user_root` exists for.

**Owning a shared root, and the reason this record used to decline it.** Five of the seven products read this root, and the decline said: *a namespace is removed whole, so a second declaration would make either provider's remove take the other's skills.* That sentence was true when it was written and stopped being true when `written_paths` shipped -- `remove` under this scope takes the files this provider recorded writing and refuses rather than widening when it cannot read the record, and each harness carries its own state file, so they coexist under one root. The reason was not re-read when the thing it described changed.

Relative to this scope's own root the path is `skills`, not `.agents/skills`: the root is what the scope names, and writing it into the path again would put the skills at `~/.agents/.agents/skills`.

**Re-asked at 1.0.18 on 2026-09-04.** Digest-verified `grok-1.0.18-linux-x86_64` (`sha256:42f6efb4…`), `grok inspect --json` in a temporary HOME: the same `skills/` probe is still `source.type=user`.

declined.reason: Grok 1.0.18 discovers `~/.agents/commands/<name>.md` as a **skill**, in the same `skills` array as `~/.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`. Measured with `grok inspect --json` against a temporary HOME on the digest-verified `grok-1.0.18-linux-x86_64`: `nddev-agents-command.md` appeared as `skills[].name=nddev-agents-command` with `source.type=user`; a control file under `$HOME/.agents-not-a-root/commands/` did not. The owned `skills` surface already routes the skill kind under this scope. Owning `commands` too would put one kind on two surfaces, which `harness_runtime::surfaces` refuses. This provider writes user-root skills only under `skills/`. The vendor page names both directories; the run is what decided they are one kind.
declined.source: https://docs.x.ai/build/features/skills-plugins-marketplaces; measured by running grok 1.0.18 inspect --json against a temporary HOME, 2026-09-04

native_surfaces.configuration_schema_note: **No machine-readable configuration schema is published, measured rather than assumed.** Every schema-looking url in the pinned `grok-1.0.13-linux-x86_64` resolves to `json-schema.org` meta-schemas and vocabularies -- the validator library's own, not a description of `config.toml`. 37 distinct urls, none of them xAI's. So the keys this estate writes are sourced from the binary and the settings reference, and there is nothing to validate them against. Surveyed 2026-08-31 across all seven; three publish one and use it, cursor publishes one it must not name, and these three publish none.

source_verified_runtime_flags_note: Read out of the 1.0.13 binary on 2026-08-31. `GROK_DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER` is documented by the product's own embedded reference, in a table of four suppression methods and their scopes, and it is the only one a launch can set without writing into a person's configuration file. A falsy value counts as not set, so launch overwrites rather than leaves an inherited `0` in place. `native_declaration_names_the_switch_it_sets` ties `updates_off_env` to this list.

surface_presence.method: Every namespace this harness declares, global and scoped, searched as a fixed string in the artifact the current pin names, digest verified before reading; both the declared path and its last segment counted, because a product that composes a path by joining segments never spells the whole of it. A count here is a lower bound and not a routing proof -- what it answers is whether a surface vanished from the product. This pin did not move on 2026-09-02 when five others did; the sweep covers all seven so the next bump has something to differ from. The invented control was searched in the same run and found nowhere, so the search discriminates. The artifact is a single executable, so the search reads its bytes directly: unpacking it yields nothing, and a search of nothing answers absent for every name -- which is what the first run of this sweep reported for this harness before the subject was named explicitly.
